title: Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies — Frank Coyle, UC Berkeley

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 87%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is structuring agent tool-use loops with an external ontology validation layer as a control-plane guardrail around the model. The neurosymbolic validation framework applies to any agent system; e-commerce examples are illustrative rather than defining a vertical. Introduces neurosymbolic concepts, demonstrates RDFS/OWL inference and the Claude tool use loop, and prescribes a practical Pydantic-plus-ontology validation pattern. Requires Python familiarity and general AI awareness but remains accessible to practitioners without deep formal-logic background. A 20-minute conference talk with slides, code demonstration, and philosophical framing. All selected evidence is directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Frank Coyle opens with an educator's philosophy from Sister Corita Kent and John Cage: 'Nothing is a mistake. There is no win. There's no fail. There's only make.' He traces two lineages converging in modern AI: agents (McCarthy, Selfridge, Minsky, 1956) and ontologies (Aristotle, Gruber's 1993 'formal specification of a shared conceptualization'). Their convergence is neurosymbolic AI—probabilistic LLMs paired with symbolic knowledge graphs. Coyle argues hallucination is a feature of LLMs, not a bug, and ontologies keep models on guardrails. He defines ontologies as graph structures of entities, relationships, and properties, more flexible than relational databases. Building can be top-down or bottom-up; existing taxonomies like schema.org, FOAF, Dublin Core, and DBpedia should be reused. RDFS provides domain/range inference; OWL adds transitive and functional properties for inference and constraints. He connects agent loops to Bohm and Jacopini's 1966 Turing completeness result, warning loops can break, drift, and accumulate cost. He then walks through a Claude tool use loop: the LLM proposes tool calls with parameters but cannot execute them; the system checks the stop reason, executes the tool, and validates results against an ontology before acting. Pydantic checks parameter types at the door; the ontology checks results at the ledger. Agents should avoid side effects until ontology validation passes. Specific errors ontologies catch that English cannot: a second refund on the same order (functional property), a payout sent to the support desk instead of the buyer (OWL disjoint property distinguishing customer from support rep), and invented status values like 'probably shipped' (constrained enumerations of paid, shipped, refunded). He closes by reiterating his philosophy and sharing his website codesupreme.ai.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Neurosymbolic AI pairs probabilistic LLMs with symbolic ontologies to keep agents on guardrails.
LLMs can only predict the next word—they cannot execute tools; the system must check stop reasons and execute tool calls on their behalf.
Pydantic validates parameter types at the door; the ontology validates results at the ledger before any side effects occur.
Agents should avoid side effects until ontology validation passes, keeping logic clean and preventing premature database changes.
OWL disjoint properties catch entity confusion errors like routing a buyer payout to a support rep.
Functional properties catch duplicate actions like a second refund on the same order.
Constrained enumerations prevent invented status values like 'probably shipped'—only paid, shipped, or refunded are valid.
Existing taxonomies (schema.org, FOAF, Dublin Core, DBpedia) should be reused rather than reinvented.
Agent loops provide Turing completeness but risk breaking, drifting, and accumulating token costs.
Understand neurosymbolic AI as combining probabilistic LLMs with symbolic ontologies

sections.title: Intro and educator's philosophy
sections.summary: Coyle introduces himself as a Berkeley educator with 30-35 years in CS, notes AI's disruption of CS career paths, and shares Sister Corita Kent's philosophy popularized by John Cage: 'Nothing is a mistake. There is no win. There's no fail. There's only make.' He advocates hands-on creation and analog writing over typing for deeper learning.

sections.title: Two lineages: agents and ontologies
sections.summary: Traces agents to early AI (McCarthy, Selfridge, Minsky, 1956) and ontologies to Aristotle's categories of being, Von Quine, and Gruber's 1993 definition of ontology as 'a formal specification of a shared conceptualization.' Introduces neurosymbolic AI as the convergence of probabilistic agents with formal symbolic representations.

sections.title: Neurosymbolic AI and hallucination as feature
sections.summary: Argues neurosymbolic AI keeps LLMs on guardrails. Hallucination is a feature of LLMs—they imagine things that may not exist, analogous to human imagination. Ontologies provide the symbolic structure to constrain this probabilistic behavior.

sections.title: What an ontology is and how to build one
sections.summary: Defines ontologies as graphs of entities, relationships, and properties, contrasting with restrictive relational databases. Covers top-down (expert-driven) and bottom-up (interaction-driven) construction. Recounts the expert systems era of the 1980s that couldn't scale, leading to AI winter, and neural networks that eventually scaled with GPUs.

sections.title: Reusing existing taxonomies
sections.summary: Recommends reusing existing taxonomies developed over 15-20 years: schema.org, FOAF for social networks, Dublin Core for research documents, and DBpedia which underlies Wikipedia searches.

sections.title: RDFS and OWL: inference and constraints
sections.summary: Explains RDFS domain and range for inference (teaches has domain teacher, range student) and OWL properties: transitive (ancestor) for chain inference and functional (has father) for uniqueness constraints. These sit alongside the graph, augmenting it with derived data and constraints.

sections.title: Agents, loops, and how they break
sections.summary: Connects agent loops to Bohm and Jacopini's 1966 result that sequence, conditionals, and loops make a language Turing complete. Warns loops can break via infinite iteration, drift between agents, and accumulating token costs. Frames current agentic AI as revisiting symbolic AI and expert systems.

sections.title: Beginning of Claude agent code demonstration
sections.summary: Begins showing a Python Claude agent example with a while-true loop, mentioning a client and model response, but the code demonstration is cut off at the section boundary.

sections.title: Claude tool use loop with ontology validator
sections.summary: Explains the tool use loop: LLMs can only predict next words and cannot execute tools, so they return parameters and a stop reason. The system checks the stop reason, executes the tool, and validates results against an ontology. If results are unreasonable, it loops back to the LLM or brings a human in the loop. Pydantic checks parameter types at the door; the ontology checks results at the ledger. Agents should avoid side effects until validation passes.

sections.title: Errors an ontology catches that English cannot
sections.summary: Shows specific OWL constructs and the errors they catch: functional properties prevent a second refund on the same order; disjoint properties distinguish customer from support rep, catching misrouted payouts; constrained enumerations prevent invented status values like 'probably shipped,' allowing only paid, shipped, or refunded. Closes by reiterating the 'nothing is a mistake' philosophy and sharing his website codesupreme.ai.

demonstrations: RDFS domain/range inference example: 'Bob teaches Scooter' infers Bob is a teacher (and person), Scooter is a student
OWL transitive property example: Sue ancestor of Mary, Mary ancestor of Ann, infers Sue ancestor of Ann
OWL functional property example: has father is functional—only one father allowed, so Bob and BB refer to same individual
Claude agent tool use loop: LLM proposes tool call parameters, system checks stop reason, executes tool, validates results against ontology before acting
Pydantic at the door, ontology at the ledger: type-check inputs with Pydantic, validate outputs against domain ontology
limitations: Expert systems of the 1980s could not scale, leading to AI winter
